## Overview
The Prometheus' Architecture is a foundational framework for a metamathematical reasoning system. It is designed to contain the expressive power of ZFC set theory while bridging the reasoning levels of rigorous mathematical logic and human-level reasoning. The architecture is built upon a set of primitives and constructions that allow for the representation and manipulation of mathematical objects and concepts, with the goal of creating a system that creates models for the world around it.

## Program Structure
Mathematical objects exist (primarily as sets) within a graph structure, with relationships and operations between them. Deductive reasoning (logical inference) is done via mathematical rules, which can model all the number systems and strategies useful for inductive/statistical reasoning. ...

## Primitives
* Sets (constant, variable-constant, and variable. The program will attempt to classify everything in terms of constant or variable sets)
  + Constant type set: {}C (represents a collection as a single object)
  + Variable-constant type set: {}VC (represents a possibility space of an unknown single object)
  + Variable type set: {}V (represents a collection of objects as an abstraction over all members of the collection)

### Standard set theory foundation constructions, with constant sets:
:::{}
* Intersection      &nbsp;&nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp;&nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; $A \cap B = \{x \mid x \in A \text{ and } x \in B\}C$
A∩B = {x | x∈A and x∈B}C
* Union             &nbsp;&nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp;&nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp;&nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp;&nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; A∪B = {x | x∈A or x∈B}C
* Power Set         &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp;&nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; 𝒫(A) = {X | X⊆A}C
* Predicate Subset  &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; {x | P(x)}C = {x | x∈A and P(x)}C
* Cartesian Product &nbsp; &nbsp;&nbsp; A×B = {(a,b) | a∈A and b∈B}C
* Function Mapping  &nbsp; &nbsp;&nbsp; f(A) = {f(x) | x∈A}C
:::

::: {.list-grid}
- **Intersection**
  - $A \cap B = \{x \mid x \in A \text{ and } x \in B\}C$

- **Union**
  - $A \cup B = \{x \mid x \in A \text{ or } x \in B\}C$

- **Power Set**
  - $\mathcal{P}(A) = \{X \mid X \subseteq A\}C$

- **Predicate Subset**
  - $\{x \mid P(x)\}C = \{x \mid x \in A \text{ and } P(x)\}C$

- **Cartesian Product**
  - $A \times B = \{(a,b) \mid a \in A \text{ and } b \in B\}C$

- **Function Mapping**
  - $f(A) = \{f(x) \mid x \in A\}C$
:::


As well as extending set theory formulations that build up set theory constructively:

:::{}
* Disjoint Union    A⊎B = {AX{0}C ∪ BX{1}C}C
* Relation          R⊆A×B = { (a,b) | a∈A and b∈B }C
* Function          f:A→B = { (a,b) | a∈A and b∈B and f(a)=b }C [^2]
* etc.

[^2]: with the additional constraint that for all a∈A, there exists a unique b∈B such that (a,b)∈f; that is, one input maps to only one output

### Ambiguity and Possibility constructions, with variable-constant sets:
* **Impossibility:          NA = {}VC**
* Tautology:             x = {x}VC
: A single possibility must be the true value
* Possibility compilation {A={...}VC, B={...}VC}VC = {AUB}VC
: If two sets of possibilities are possible, then any of the possibilities from either set are possible
* Ambiguous Component:    f({...}VC) = {f(...)}VC
: A VC set with type X members can be used as a component in any construction, object method, or operation that requires a type X member. Operation and object method results will be a VC set as a collection of evaluation outcomes for each member. E.g. {3, 4}%3 = {0,1} E.g. length({“12”, 12}) = {2, NA}


### Abstraction with variable sets:


:::::

Also, for any set that can be validly constructed as one type of set, its intension is valid for the other types of sets. E.g. {1,2,3}C ⇔ {1,2,3}VC ⇔ {1,2,3}V. 


## Starting Axioms and Template Structures:
::::: {.panel-tabset}
### Axioms
* **Axiom of Intensionality** By definition, any two sets with the same intension are the same object. Since x=x always, pairing this with the axiom of extensionality means the object(s) has the same elements (as itself). "==" is used to denote not only equality but identicality, which might be expressed as equality in every equivalence relation, or every possible measure.
: ∀x ∀y (x.intension = y.intension → x == y)
* **Axiom of Extensionality** Two sets are equal if and only if they have exactly the same elements.
: ∀x ∀y (∀z (z ∈ x ↔ z ∈ y) → x = y)
* **Axiom of Foundation (Regularity)** No non-empty set S contains any set that contains members of themself (S). Prevents direct self-containment, looping chains of self-containment, and infinite chains of membership. **Need to explore**
∀x (∃y (y ∈ x) → ∃y (y ∈ x ∧ ∀z ¬(z ∈ y ∧ z ∈ x)))
Equivalently: ∀x(x/{} → ∃y∈ x(y ∩ x = {}))
* **Axiom Schema of Separation (Specification)** A property-defined subset of a set forms a set.
For every formula φ(x, w₁, …, wₙ) in which y is not free:  
∀w₁ … ∀wₙ ∀A ∃B ∀x (x ∈ B ↔ (x ∈ A ∧ φ(x, w₁, …, wₙ)))
* **Axiom of Pairing** You can define a set that contains exactly two existing sets as members.
∀u ∀v ∃p ∀w (w ∈ p ↔ (w = u ∨ w = v))
* **Axiom of Union** You can define a set as the members of the member-sets in a set of sets. Defines a n-operand version of the Union operation.
∀C ∃U ∀x (x ∈ U ↔ ∃S (S ∈ C ∧ x ∈ S))
* **Axiom of Power Set** You can define a set of all the subsets of an existing set.
∀X ∃P ∀Y (Y ∈ P ↔ ∀z (z ∈ Y → z ∈ X))
* **Axiom of Infinity** There is a set that contains every layer of set: {}, {{}}, {{{}}}, etc., represents inductive sets. The smallest such set (the intersection of all inductive sets) is the set ω of natural numbers in the von Neumann representation.
∃I (∅ ∈ I ∧ ∀x (x ∈ I → x ∪ {x} ∈ I))
* **Axiom Schema of Replacement** The result of mapping each element of a set with a function produces a new set. Implies Separation?
For every formula φ(x, y, w₁, …, wₙ):  
∀w₁ … ∀wₙ ∀A (∀x ∈ A ∃!y φ(x, y, …) → ∃B ∀x ∈ A ∃y ∈ B φ(x, y, …))

**3.9 Axiom of Choice**  
∀C (∅ ∉ C → ∃f (f is a function ∧ dom(f) = C ∧ ∀S ∈ C (f(S) ∈ S)))
**3.10 Empty Set / Set Existence** (often listed for emphasis)  
∃x ∀y ¬(y ∈ x)  
  or simply  
∃x (x = x)

* **Empty Set.** ∀x ∈ {}C is false.
* **Constant Membership.** For any (of the three types of) set X ∈ C and element e, either e ∈ X or e ∉ X (law of excluded middle for membership).
* **Ambiguous Membership.** {x1, x2, ..., xn}CV ∈ X means that one of the xi is a member of X, but we don't know which one: x1 ∈ X or x2 ∈ X or ... or xn ∈ X. 
* **Abstract Membership.** {x1, x2, ..., xn}V ∈ X means that all of the xi are members of X: x1 ∈ X and x2 ∈ X and ... and xn ∈ X. Alternately, the extension of the variable set interpretted as a constant set is a subset: {x1, x2, ..., xn}C ⊆ X.
* **Constant Extensionality.** For any (of the three types of) sets A, B: A = B ⟺ ∀x (x ∈ A ↔ x ∈ B). For C, this means the constant sets are identical — they contain exactly the same elements in their extension. For VC, this means the possibility spaces are identical — they contain exactly the same set of possible values. For V, they abstract over the same collection of members.
* **Proposition Formation.** Any well-formed formula P(x) evaluates to a truth value {True, False} for each x in its domain. Note that {}VC denotes impossibility, or NA. When this represents possibilities that could evaluate to True, it may implie the falsity of a proposition, but it is not a truth value itself and must be treated in context.
* **Boolean Logic** -- **Needs further exploring with** See the Template Structure for the other part.
 + Binary/Bivalent (for universal **Logic Predicates**, see note on Predicates below)
  - Negation ¬φ — True when φ is False, False when φ is True
  - Conjunction φ ∧ ψ — True precisely when both φ and ψ are True.
  - Disjunction φ ∨ ψ — True precisely when at least one of φ, ψ is True (inclusive).
  - Implication φ → ψ — equivalent to ¬φ ∨ ψ; False only when φ is True and ψ is False.
  - Biconditional φ ↔ ψ — equivalent to (φ → ψ) ∧ (ψ → φ).
 + **Reminder:** non-sets are treated as constants, and the result of an operation with a VC is a VC of the outputs of the operation. If this results in a single member within the VC, recall the rule {x}VC = x.
* **Logical Inference** -- **Needs further exploring with**
  + Modus Ponens: given P and P→Q, infer Q
  + Modus Tollens: given !Q and P→Q, infer ¬P (for binary, double-check for Set Predicates)
  + Generalization: given φ, infer ∀x φ (research "free-variable restrictions")
  + Equality Rules:
   - reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, and substitution of equals
  
  
* **Quantifiers, including Bound as Shorthand**
 + Universal Quantifier: ∀x φ(x) — “for every x, φ(x) holds.”
 + Existential Quantifier: ∃x φ(x) — “there exists at least one x such that φ(x) holds.”
 + Unique Existence:  ∃!x φ(x) — abbreviation for ∃x (φ(x) ∧ ∀y (φ(y) → y = x)) — "there exists an x such that φ(x) holds and any y for which φ(y) holds is equal to x", so x is the only unique object that satisfies φ.
 + Bounded quantifiers are convenient abbreviations:
  - ∀x ∈ A φ(x) means ∀x (x ∈ A → φ(x))
  - ∃x ∈ A φ(x) means ∃x (x ∈ A ∧ φ(x))
 + **Note** Predicate Quantifiers check for "Truth" values unless specified ("P(x) holds"="P(x) is True", "P(x) does not hold"="P(x) is not True"="P(x) is False or NA", whereas "P(x) is False" is True only when the value is False, and is False when the value is either True or NA) 



### Starting Template Structures (minimal building blocks, rules, or strategies)
* Empty set (all three set types): {}C, {}VC, {}V (this last one I'm not sure about -- it might be logically valid but not very meaningful or useful...). Empty Set is supposedly derivable from the axioms of Infinity and Separation. 
* Unknown specific object: {x∈X}VC defines an unknown object from the collection X, allowing definition from limited information. {x∉{}C}VC defines an unknown object that isn't in the empty set, allowing the definition of a completely unknown object.
* Unknown abstract object: {x∈X}V defines a representation of any/all objects from the collection X, allowing definition from limited information. {x∉{}C}V defines the most extreme abstraction, representing any and all objects.
* **Boolean Logic** -- **Needs further exploring with** See the Axioms list for the other part.
 + Trinary/Trivalent (for general logic and **Set Predicates** that might not be defined, see note on Predicates below)
  - Negation ¬φ — "True or NA" when φ is False, "False or NA" when φ is True, "True or False" when φ is NA. These values, "X" and "Y", are expressed as a possibility state with a variable-constant set: {X, Y}VC. They are not to be confused with the compound propositions, e.g. True OR False, which would be True.
  - Conjunction φ ∧ ψ — True precisely when both φ and ψ are True. NA when at least one is NA (inclusive). Otherwise False.
  - Disjunction φ ∨ ψ — True precisely when at least one of φ, ψ is True (inclusive). False otherwise (NAs give as much information as False)
  - Implication φ → ψ — **Needs refinement**. 
    - If equivalent to ¬φ ∨ ψ; then True if ψ is True or φ is False, otherwise False when φ is True (like binary logic), but {True, False}VC when φ is NA. 
    - If not strictly equivalent to ¬φ ∨ ψ; then φ being NA might more appropriately be NA.
  false only when φ is true and ψ is false.
  - Biconditional φ ↔ ψ — equivalent to (φ → ψ) ∧ (ψ → φ), presumably. 
    - I think should evaluate as False unless both inputs are True or both inputs are False, intuitively.
    - Using the definition of ¬φ ∨ ψ for implication and the biconditional as a conjunction of two implications, it should be True when the inputs match as either True or False, otherwise if one of the inputs is True, then False (the same as before), but when one input is NA and the other is not True (False or NA), then the output is True/False, {True, False}VC.
    - Using a conjunction of implications not strictly equivalent to ¬φ ∨ ψ, (instead defining φ → ψ as NA when φ is NA) then φ ↔ ψ is NA when at least one input is NA (inclusive), otherwise it is the same as the binary biconditional.
  - **For Now, this system will use all of the above**. The different implications and biconditionals will be available as proposition/rules, but none of the trinary alternatives will be considered "True" axiomatically until further notice. We should remember that NA is not ambiguity or an unknown value like {True, False}VC -- NA is a non-answer, the absence of an answer, used when a question is ill-formed or something doesn't have a truth value.
 + **Reminder:** non-sets are treated as constants, and the result of an operation with a VC is a VC of the outputs of the operation. If this results in a single member within the VC, recall the rule {x}VC = x.


### Drafting
Progression Axioms:
1. Some first object exists (e.g., 0)
2. Every object has a successor, which is also an object.
3. No two objects have the same successor
4. The first object is not the successor of any object.
5. If a property is possessed by the first object and also by the successor of every object that has that property, then it is possessed by all objects (including classifications and memberships).

This is a generalization of Peano's Axioms:
1. 0 is a number.
2. Every number has a successor, which is also a number.
3. No two numbers have the same successor
4. 0 is not the successor of any number.
5. If a property is possessed by 0 and also by the successor of every number that has that property, then it is possessed by all numbers. 
* Endless sequence of unique numbers (via 2 and 3) that don't loop (via 4), which includes all numbers (via 5).
* "Ordinal arithmetic" -- m+n is defined using m+0=m and m+(n+1)=S(m+n), reducing recursion. Defines addition and equivalents for progressions.

* Some mechanism of mapping between sets to compare their cardinality, allowing the definition of numbers as equivalence classes of sets with equal cardinality. (One-one relation identification with the two sets as domain and codomain.)

## Misc Notes:
* Set-typing; indicates membership of a constant or subsetting of constant-variable or variable sets in relation to the Constant "type" set. Useful for defining allowed domains and behaviors. Adds "types" but in a more intuitive approach, allowing a term to belong to multiple types. X is of settype A means: X is a Constant as a member of A or X is either a VC set or variable set as a subset of A.
* **Note on Predicates** A predicate as defined as a truth-value-mapping function can return three values for a given evaluation: True (input maps to True), False (input maps to False), or NA (input is not in the domain), unless the domain of a predicate includes all objects. This latter option is when this notion of predicate aligns with the classical first-order predicate requirement of evaluating to exactly either True or False. Layering an additional mapping that brings NA to False, or adding that mapping functionality to a conditional in the predicate definition can yield a first-order-compatible True/False predicate. These might be termed **Set Predicates** and **Logic Predicates** respectively (again, both are sets encoding truth-value functions, but one has a limited domain and the other is universal).
* **Note on Existence** To exist as an idea, an object need only exist with a definition in memory -- this could include any concept in theory -- and sets are defined by intension. So the set of all numbers greater than 3 and less than 2 exists as a concept, but it has no extension. Thus, most colloquial language on existence refers to the extension of a set, and the idea of something -- even something abstract like an idea -- existing is dealing with the membership of the extension. Unicorns, for instance, exist as an idea, and being logically consistent (as far as being a horse with a horn is concerned), the extension can be non-empty, including all possible fictional unicorns (such as fictional characters) or real unicorns (if surgery, genetic engineering, or unexpected circumstance permitted a nonfictional example). The statement "unicorns aren't real", would then be best understood as a statement with an implied restriction of scope to the known physical universe, within which the intension has no extension (to the author's knowledge). Thus, conceptual (by intensional definition), theoretical (by general extensional definition), and specific (by extensional definition restricted by scope) existence can be considered.

* Equivalence Relations are Reflexive (A-A), Symmetric (A-B <-> B-A), and Transitive (A-B & B-C -> A-C)
* Partial Order is Relation that's Reflexive, Transitive, and Antisymmetric (A<=B and B<=A -> A=B) *Is this relative to an equivalence relation (two objects are the same value), or is it a statement of two objects being the same (creating an implication that there cannot be two objects with the same value)?
* A total order (or linear order) is a partial order where every pair of distinct elements can be compared
* Domain theory uses partial orders and directed sets. A directed set is a collection where any two elements have an upper bound in the collection. Every directed set must have a least upper bound (supremum) in the domain. This captures the idea that infinite approximations converge to a limit.
+ Continuous functions: Functions between domains that preserve the approximation structure - if you have better approximations to inputs, you get better approximations to outputs. Formally, they preserve suprema of directed sets.
+ Scott topology: A special topology (way of defining "open sets") on domains where the open sets are precisely those preserved by taking suprema of directed sets. This makes continuous functions in the domain sense correspond to continuous functions in the topological sense.



* System switching will be an advanced mechanic added in later. For now, I want to make sure basic propositional logic, FO predicate logic and set theory can be instantiated, sufficient to define relations, finite and infinite systems of objects (like the natural numbers), basic arithmetic, etc. 

* This system should in large part be inspired by (and perhaps structured as a compilation of) various existing logical programs, but should have as a key design aspect the process and goal of using mathematical principles to classify and model inputs and data patterns, e.g. seeing that words correspond to patterns that could be mapped to values and an operation in a system so that "one plus one equals" aligns with "1+1=" and "two" aligns with "2" in usage patterns. The system should be very clear about what is and what isn't, so the above example could be mapped to a wide range of systems (without knowledge of standard English or math notation), but the more information provided narrows down the patterns of what "one plus one equals" could mean. Also progressions vs number systems vs the natural numbers would be notable distinctions for the user -- progressions can be defined using a few axioms, number systems would be a bit trickier to define rigorously, and the natural numbers would be a progression that aligns with the specific values that we'd want for standard math, maybe expressible in terms of set ordinals, e.g. Von Neumann ordinals (idk if this really indicates the natural numbers inherently even though it works pretty intuitively as a representation of them once you learn about them). 

* Cox's theorem (the classical justification for why probability theory is the unique consistent extension of Boolean logic to degrees of plausibility)
* On unifying ZFC + category theory + topos theory into one foundation: 
 + **ETCS** (Elementary Theory of the Category of Sets) — Lawvere, 1964. Axiomatizes "the category of Sets" using purely categorical primitives: it's a topos that is additionally well-pointed, has choice, and has a natural numbers object (which forces it to be Boolean/classical). This is probably the best template if you want the combined-foundations approach (option a) rather than the single-abstract-foundation approach (option b).
 + Logical framework architecture — a small trusted meta-calculus (typically a dependently-typed core) serves as the "abstract foundation," and each target system (propositional logic, FOL, set theory, category theory, topos theory) is represented as an object logic — an encoding living inside that kernel, via "judgments as types" (Edinburgh LF, Automath). **Isabelle** is a working existence proof of exactly this
 + Univalent Foundations / **HoTT** — types-as-spaces, where ordinary sets fall out as a special case (types with no higher path structure, "h-sets") and category-theoretic structure is native (∞-groupoids are the objects of higher category theory). Deepest unification, hardest to implement well — still an active research frontier (see cubical type theory for a computational account of univalence).
 + My Choice: Currently I want to explore a logical framework architecture like **Isabelle**. I think what I'm looking for is model-theoretic interpretation with abductive logic programming to have Version-space/candidate-elimination narrowing, which will need formal language theory and parsing system(s) to interpret input.
